<reason>B (PRO) won the debate's spine. B's Q2 — "expecting them where?" — exposed A's core dependency, and when A answered with a list (video call, the existing library at 2 p.m., café, congregation), B's closing converted it into the decisive dilemma: the app is either a pointer to the very rooms B wants funded, or the bare screen A conceded reduces no one's anxiety. A's last-word recovery (rooms are abundant and empty; "fund more signs, not a second road") was rhetorically excellent but restated the abundance frame without repairing the list's known vulnerabilities — B had already shown, unrebutted, that the lonely can't use a 2 p.m. library (work, shifts) and that cafés charge the poor for presence. B also defused A's "10 p.m. in February" attack by redefining late hours as 6–9 p.m. with the laundromat/pharmacy observation; A never adapted. B's constituency point (app churn, digitally excluded loneliest) survived, answered only implicitly. A fought back hard: the symmetric-mediation move and the amortization answer to B's cost question were genuinely sharp, and A cleanly exploited B's clipped homebound concession. But B's two clipped turns and a slight blurring of A's anxiety/loneliness distinction are execution costs that keep this clear-but-competitive rather than dominant.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Pressure Q2 ("expecting them where — isn't your intervention's success dependent on the very budget line you'd cut?") forced A4.3's destination list, which B's closing weaponized: "An app that succeeds by sending people to a library is an argument for funding the library." A's sign/road analogy in the final speech was the best counterpunch but couldn't fully repair the 2 p.m.-library and paid-café weaknesses B had already established.</best_rebuttal>
